opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's always a pleasure to be back in China.

What impressed me most on this trip is the speed. Every time I come, the pace of iteration seems to have gone up another notch. A year or two ago, many of the humanoid and robotics teams I met were still showing carefully staged demos. This time I saw far more systems running in real environments: factories, warehouses, labs set up to collect data at scale. The ecosystem is very complete. You have the hardware supply chain, the manufacturing know-how, and a very large pool of engineers all in close proximity. That lets teams build a new robot body, test it, break it, and rebuild it in weeks rather than months. That's a real advantage.

I also noticed a shift in mindset. People increasingly recognize that the bottleneck in Physical AI isn't just the hardware or a clever control algorithm. It's data, and more specifically the right kind of data. Language models had the internet to learn from. Robots don't have an internet of physical interaction. So teams are combining several sources: real-world teleoperation data, human video, and more and more simulation and synthetic data generated by world models. That's an area I care a lot about, and it was encouraging to see so many groups taking it seriously.

That said, I think we should be honest that the whole field, not just China, is still early. We're probably in something like the GPT-2 phase for Physical AI. The demos are exciting, but robust generalization, where a robot can walk into a new home or a new factory line and just work reliably, isn't solved yet. Safety, reliability, and long-horizon reasoning in the physical world are still open problems.

So my overall assessment is very positive. The energy and engineering capacity are remarkable, and I think a lot of important progress in Physical AI will come out of this region. But the hardest scientific questions are still ahead of all of us, and that's what makes this such an exciting time to be working on it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, I came back from that trip quite impressed, and also a little bit surprised by how fast things moved since my previous visit.

The first thing that struck me is the density of hardware. In the Bay Area, if you want to build a humanoid or a quadruped, you are talking to maybe a handful of companies, and the supply chain is slow. In Shenzhen and Hangzhou, I visited labs where they could iterate on a robot body in weeks. Motors, reducers, sensors, the whole stack is local. That changes the pace of research, because in Physical AI the body and the brain co-evolve. You cannot separate them. If you can change the body quickly, you learn faster what the brain actually needs.

The second thing is the number of young teams. I met many startups led by people in their late twenties, and they are not just assembling parts. They are training their own policies, building their own data pipelines, running their own simulation. Some of the work on whole-body control and locomotion is genuinely at the frontier. I would say in locomotion specifically, China is on par with or ahead of anyone.

Where I think the gap still exists is on the foundation model side, the world-model layer. Physical AI needs models that understand physics, that can predict what happens next in a scene, that can generalize across many embodiments. That requires enormous scale of compute and data, and compute is of course the constraint everyone talks about. Several teams told me very directly that their bottleneck is not talent, it is GPUs. So they are being very clever about efficiency, about distillation, about using simulation to stretch every bit of compute they have. In some ways that pressure is producing interesting research.

The third observation is about data. Everyone has realized that the internet does not contain robot data the way it contains text. So the question becomes, how do you manufacture it. I saw teleoperation farms with dozens of operators collecting demonstrations, and I saw heavy investment in simulation and synthetic data. My own view is that simulation plus world models is the scalable path, and I was glad to see that many groups in China share that belief rather than relying purely on human teleoperation, which does not scale.

If I had to summarize, I would say the manufacturing ecosystem and the engineering energy are world-class, the control and locomotion research is at the frontier, and the main open question is whether the model and compute layer can keep up. The people I met are very aware of that, and they are moving very fast. I would not bet against them.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate what looks impressive in a demonstration from what works reliably in the real world. With Physical AI, the important question is whether a system can handle variation—different objects, unfamiliar environments, unexpected situations—and recover when something goes wrong.

I don’t have specific observations from that visit in this conversation to draw on, so I wouldn’t want to invent examples. But that’s the lens I’d use to assess progress in China: how consistently these systems can perform useful tasks, how much human intervention they need, and how quickly experience translates into better performance.

I’d assess progress by looking at how well systems perform in the physical world: can they perceive what’s happening, adapt when conditions change, and complete a useful task reliably? A compelling demonstration is one milestone; sustained operation is another.

The conversation hasn’t established what I saw on that visit, so I can’t give you specific firsthand examples. But the questions I’d focus on are reliability, how much human intervention is needed, and whether the system can generalize beyond the environment it was trained in. Those are the measures that would tell me how much progress is translating into practical capability.
